title: What custom software actually costs in India, and what moves the number
excerpt: Nobody publishes real numbers, so buyers guess and quotes vary by 10x for the same brief. Here is how the pricing actually works, what makes it move, and the questions that stop you overpaying.

body.text: Ask five software studios what a project costs and you will get five numbers that do not overlap. One quotes two lakh, one quotes forty. Both are describing the same brief. That spread is not dishonesty, it is the absence of a shared unit, and it leaves buyers with no way to tell a fair price from a bad one.
So here is how the pricing works underneath, written plainly, from a studio that quotes fixed price and therefore has to be right about this.
The only thing that actually drives cost is screens and rules

Software cost is not driven by the technology. It is driven by two things: how many distinct screens a person has to be able to use, and how many rules sit behind them. A screen that lists records is cheap. A screen that lists records, filters them six ways, lets three roles edit different fields, locks after approval, and emails somebody when a date passes, is not one screen. It is a week.
When you read a quote, count the screens the proposal names. If it names four and you can think of nine, the quote is not for your project.
The honest bands
These are the ranges we see in the Indian market for work that is built properly, handed over, and does not need the builder in order to keep running.

items: A single internal tool, one or two roles, six to ten screens: roughly 1.5 to 4 lakh. An approvals tracker, an inspection app, a stock register.
A full web application with several roles, a dashboard and an integration: roughly 4 to 12 lakh. This is the bulk of what mid sized businesses need.
A platform with external users, payments, and compliance requirements: 12 lakh and up, and the number depends almost entirely on the compliance part.
An ERP or CRM integration on its own: 1 to 5 lakh, depending entirely on whether the system on the far end has a real API.

body.text: Anything materially below those bands is being delivered by someone who intends to make the money back on changes, maintenance or by handing you a codebase nobody can take over. That is not a cheaper project. It is a deferred invoice.
What makes the number go up, in order
If you want to control the price, these are the levers, strongest first.

items: Number of user roles. Each role is a different set of permissions, a different screen layout and a different test case. Going from one role to three can add half the project.
Approval chains. A field that one person edits is trivial. A field that routes through two approvers, can be rejected, reopened and must keep a history, is a module.
Integrations with systems you do not control. The cost is not the code, it is the waiting. If the vendor's API is undocumented, or access needs their consultant, the schedule belongs to them.
Offline use. Working without signal means queuing, syncing and conflict resolution. It is worth it when crews work on sites, and it is money wasted when everyone sits in an office.
Reporting that must be exactly right. Dashboards are cheap. Dashboards that must reconcile to the rupee with your accounting system are not.
Migration of old data. Clean data is a day. Fifteen years of inconsistent spreadsheets is a fortnight, and it is nobody's favourite work.

body.text: What does not move the number as much as people think

Design quality barely changes the cost, because the work is in the thinking rather than the pixels. Nor does the choice of framework. And nor, mostly, does the number of records: a system holding ten thousand rows and one holding ten million are the same build until you get to serious scale.

The thing buyers most often pay extra for without benefit is a feature list assembled by asking everyone what they want. Half of it is never used. A good studio will cut that list in the scoping call, and the cut is worth more to you than the discount you were going to negotiate.
Fixed price or hourly

Hourly billing moves every risk onto you. If the estimate was wrong, you pay for it. If the developer is slow, you pay for it. If the scope was vague, you pay for the conversation. The incentive points the wrong way, and everyone involved knows it.

Fixed price moves that risk to the studio, which is where it belongs, because they are the ones who can estimate. The honest version has a written scope, a named date and a clear statement of what is not included. The dishonest version has a low headline and a change request for every sentence you did not think to write down.
The question that separates them: ask what happens if the build takes twice as long as they thought. If the answer costs you money, it is not fixed price.
The questions that save you the most money
Before you compare quotes, ask every studio the same six things. The answers will tell you more than the numbers.

items: What is explicitly not included in this price?
Who owns the code and where does the repository live?
What happens if we want a change halfway through?
What does support cost after launch, and what does it cover?
Can we see something working before the final week?
If we wanted to move to another developer in a year, what would that take?

body.text: The last question is the one that reveals most. A studio that has built for handover answers it in a sentence. A studio that has built for lock in starts explaining why you would never want to.
A rule of thumb that holds up

Work out what the current process costs you in time. Hours a week, multiplied by what those hours are worth, multiplied by fifty. If the software costs less than one year of that, it is almost always worth building. If it costs more than two years of it, the scope is too big and should be cut rather than financed.

That calculation has killed more of our own proposals than any competitor has. We would rather lose a project than build something that does not pay for itself, because the ones that do not pay are also the ones that get abandoned, and an abandoned system is worse than the spreadsheet it replaced.

title: How to choose a software development company, and the questions that reveal the truth
excerpt: Every studio says the same things on their website. These are the questions that actually separate the ones who will finish from the ones who will not.

body.text: Every software company's website says the same four things. Experienced team. Agile process. Quality delivery. Client focused. None of it is false and none of it is useful, because the company that will disappear in week six says it too.
What follows is how to tell them apart. It is written by a studio that gets compared, so read it knowing that, and use it on us as well.
Look at what they refuse to do

A studio that takes every project is a studio with no opinion, and a studio with no opinion will build whatever you ask for, including the wrong thing. Ask what kind of work they turn down. If the answer is nothing, they are selling capacity, not judgement.
The best signal you can get in a first call is being told you do not need the thing you asked for. It costs them the project and it tells you everything.
Ask who writes the code

In a lot of agencies, the person in the sales call is not the person who builds, and the person who builds is not the person you will get in month two. Ask directly: who writes this, and will I talk to them? Then ask what happens if that person leaves.
Small studios win on this and lose on capacity. Large ones win on capacity and lose on continuity. Neither is wrong, but you should know which trade you are making.
Make them show you something unfinished

Polished case studies prove they can design a case study. Ask to see a project mid build, or a weekly build link from a current client with the name removed. The ones who work in the open will shrug and show you. The ones who work behind a curtain will explain why they cannot, and that explanation is the answer.
The scope conversation is the real interview

Watch what happens when you describe your process. A studio that is listening will interrupt with awkward questions: what happens when the approver is on leave, what do you do today when the number is wrong, who checks this. A studio that is selling will nod and start describing features.
You are not buying code. You are buying somebody's understanding of your process, and the quality of their questions is the only evidence of it you will get before you sign.
Eight questions worth asking all of them

items: What is not included in this price, specifically?
What have you built that is closest to this, and what went wrong on it?
Who owns the code, and whose account is the repository in?
What do we see at the end of week one, and week two?
If we change our mind about something in week three, what happens?
Who do I call six months after launch, and what does that cost?
What would make you tell us this project is a bad idea?
What do you need from us, and what happens to the date if we are slow?

body.text: The second question is the most revealing and the most avoided. Every real project has something that went wrong. A studio that cannot name one has either not built much or is not going to be honest with you when it happens on yours.
Red flags that are worth walking away from

items: A quote arriving without a scoping conversation. They are guessing, and the correction will be your problem.
A price that is dramatically below everyone else. The money comes back through change requests or it does not come back at all, and neither ends well.
Unwillingness to put the scope in writing. Everything that is not written down is a disagreement waiting for a deadline.
The code living in their account, not yours.
A proposal full of technology names and empty of your process. They are describing themselves, not you.
No mention at all of what happens after launch.

body.text: The last one matters more than the rest

Most software does not fail at launch. It fails eleven months later, when the person who understood it has left, the thing nobody documented breaks, and the studio that built it is busy with somebody else. Ask about month twelve in the first call. The answer tells you whether they are building you an asset or a dependency.

title: Seven signs your business has outgrown spreadsheets
excerpt: Spreadsheets do not fail loudly. They get slower, more fragile and more dependent on one person, until a number is wrong at the worst possible moment. Here is how to spot it early.

body.text: Nothing has done more for small business than the spreadsheet, and nothing has quietly cost growing businesses more. The problem is never the spreadsheet itself. It is that it keeps working just well enough, long after it stopped being the right tool, and the failure when it comes is sudden and expensive.
Here is what the last few years before that failure look like.
1. One person is the system

There is somebody who knows how the file works. They built the formulas, they know which tab not to touch, and when they are on leave something waits. That is not a spreadsheet, that is a single point of failure with a salary.
The test: if that person left tomorrow, how long before something breaks? If the answer is days rather than months, you have already outgrown it.
2. There are versions

Final. Final v2. Final updated Oct. The copy on somebody's desktop that has the right numbers. The moment a file has versions, the organisation has stopped having one truth and started having several, and reconciling them is now a job.
3. Numbers arrive at meetings and disagree

Three people bring three figures for the same thing and the first twenty minutes goes on whose is right. This is the most expensive symptom, because it is not the time lost in the meeting. It is that decisions get deferred, and deferred decisions compound.
4. The data is always a bit old

The sheet is accurate as of when it was last updated, which is Monday, or month end, or whenever somebody got to it. Everyone has quietly learned to treat it as history rather than information, and nobody says so out loud.
Information you cannot act on today is not information. It is reporting.
5. People have built private workarounds

Side spreadsheets. A WhatsApp group that is really a workflow. A notebook. These appear when the official system does not fit the real work, and they are the clearest signal you will get, because people do not build workarounds for fun. They build them because they have to.
Go and find them. Each one is a feature specification written by the person who needed it.
6. Mistakes are found rather than prevented

A spreadsheet will let anyone type anything anywhere. The wrong date, the wrong rate, a formula overwritten with a number. Nothing stops it, so quality control becomes somebody checking afterwards, which is slower, more expensive and less reliable than simply not allowing it.
7. You cannot answer a simple question quickly

How many open items are over thirty days. Which customer is least profitable. Which site had the most failures this quarter. If the honest answer is that somebody would need a day to work it out, the data exists but the business cannot use it.
What to do about it, in order
Not all of it at once, and not by buying a large platform. The sequence that works:

items: Pick the single process that causes the most arguments. Not the biggest one, the one that generates friction.
Write down what actually happens, including the workarounds. The real process, not the one in the handbook.
Check whether an off the shelf product already does it. If one does, buy it. Honestly.
If nothing fits, build only that one process. Four weeks, one thing, used by real people.
Live with it for a month before building the next thing. The second build is always better because of what the first one taught you.

body.text: The mistake almost everyone makes is going from spreadsheets straight to a single system that does everything. It takes a year, it costs a fortune, and people go back to their spreadsheets because the new thing does not fit either. One process at a time is slower on paper and faster in practice.

title: What an ERP integration really costs, and why the estimate is usually wrong
excerpt: Connecting two systems sounds like a small job and is quoted like one. The code is rarely the problem. Here is where the time and money actually go.

body.text: Integration projects have a reputation for overrunning, and it is deserved. Not because connecting two systems is technically hard, it usually is not, but because the estimate is made against the part that is visible and the cost sits in the part that is not.
The code is the small part

Writing the thing that moves data from one system to another is a few days of work. In a typical integration, that is maybe fifteen per cent of the effort. The rest is spent on four things that nobody puts in a proposal.

items: Getting access. Credentials, sandbox environments, an API user with the right permissions. In a large ERP this can take weeks and it is not in your control.
Finding out what the data actually looks like. The documentation describes the intended data. The live system contains what fifteen years of users actually typed.
Deciding what happens when they disagree. Two systems hold the same customer with different addresses. Which wins? Somebody has to decide, and that somebody is usually in a meeting next week.
Handling failure. What happens when the far end is down, slow, or returns half an answer. This is the part that separates an integration that runs for years from one that silently stops on a Tuesday.

body.text: The question that predicts the cost
Before anyone quotes, ask one thing: does the system on the far end have a documented, supported API that we can get access to this month?

If yes, the project is small and predictable. If the answer involves a consultant, a licence upgrade, or a middleware product you do not own, the project has just changed shape and the honest response is to re-estimate, not to absorb it.

Where there is no API at all, scheduled file exchange is still a perfectly good answer. It is unglamorous, it is how a surprising amount of serious infrastructure actually works, and it is far better than a brittle screen scraper that breaks at the next upgrade.
Rough bands

items: One way sync of one object, good API: a week or two of work.
Two way sync with conflict rules: three to five weeks, and most of it is the rules.
Several objects across two systems with reconciliation and reporting: two to three months.
Anything where the far end has no API: add the time it takes their vendor to respond, which is not yours to promise.

body.text: The mistakes that cost the most

Syncing everything. Most integrations only need a handful of fields to move. Ask what decisions depend on this data, then move only what those decisions need. Every extra field is an extra thing to map, test and maintain forever.
Real time when nightly would do. Real time sounds better and costs several times more. If the business reads the number once a day, sync it once a day.

No monitoring. An integration that fails loudly is an inconvenience. An integration that fails quietly is a data corruption incident you discover at quarter end. Alerting is not a nice to have on this kind of work, it is the difference between an asset and a liability.
What a good integration proposal contains

items: The exact objects and fields moving, in a table, both directions
What happens on conflict, written as rules, not as a principle
What happens on failure, including who gets told
Who is responsible for getting API access, and what the date slips to if it is late
How it will be tested against real data rather than sample data

body.text: If a proposal does not contain the fourth item, the project has an unowned risk in it, and unowned risks become arguments. We put it in writing because the alternative is discovering in week three that nobody was chasing the vendor.

title: What an internal tool costs, and when it pays for itself
excerpt: Internal tools are the easiest investment to justify and the hardest to get approved, because the saving is spread across people rather than showing up as a line item. Here is how to do the maths.

body.text: Nobody gets promoted for building an admin panel. Internal tools sit in the backlog behind anything customer facing, and they stay there, while the cost of not having them is paid every week in small amounts by people who have stopped mentioning it.
Here is how to work out whether one is worth building, in numbers you can take to whoever signs.
The calculation
Four inputs, and you can get all of them in an afternoon by asking the people doing the work.

items: How many people touch this process
How many hours a week each of them spends on it
What an hour of their time costs, fully loaded
What proportion of that time the tool actually removes, which is never a hundred per cent and is usually between fifty and eighty

body.text: Multiply, annualise, compare to the build cost. An internal tool between one and a half and four lakh needs to save roughly four to ten hours a week across the team to pay back inside a year. In our experience most processes that have annoyed people enough to be mentioned are saving considerably more than that.
The savings nobody counts
The hours are the easy part and they understate it. The bigger returns are the ones that do not appear on a timesheet.

items: Errors prevented rather than found. One wrong rate caught at entry is worth more than a month of checking.
Decisions made this week instead of next. Latency in information is a real cost and nobody measures it.
The thing that stops being a single person's job. Resilience has a value and you discover it when they resign.
Work people stop avoiding. A process that is painful gets done late, and late has downstream costs.

body.text: When not to build
We talk clients out of internal tools regularly, and the reasons are consistent.

items: The process is about to change. Build the tool after the change, not before.
It is one person's preference rather than a team's problem. A tool for one enthusiastic user becomes shelfware when they move on.
A product already does it well. Buy it. Configure it properly. Move on.
The real problem is that nobody has decided who owns the process. Software will not decide that for you, and automating an unowned process just makes the confusion faster.

body.text: Start smaller than feels sensible

The most common failure is not a bad build, it is too large a first build. A tool with forty features takes four months, by which time the people who asked for it have lost interest and built a workaround. A tool with eight features takes three weeks, gets used, and tells you exactly what the next eight should be.
Everything we have built that is still in daily use years later started smaller than the client originally wanted. Everything that quietly died started bigger.

title: What four weeks of software development actually buys you
excerpt: Four weeks sounds like marketing. It is not, but it only works under conditions most projects do not meet. Here is exactly what fits, what does not, and what has to be true.

body.text: When we say a project ships in four weeks, the reasonable reaction is suspicion. Software has a long history of taking three times as long as promised, and a short timeline usually means a short list of things that were quietly left out.
So here is the honest version: what four weeks contains, what it does not, and the conditions that have to hold.
What fits

items: One process, done properly, end to end
Six to twelve screens, two or three user roles
A real database, real permissions, real validation
One integration, if the far end has a working API
A dashboard over the data the tool itself collects
Mobile friendly, because half the people will use it on a phone
Deployment, training and handover

body.text: What does not fit

items: Several processes at once. Each one is its own four weeks.
Integrations with systems where access has not been arranged yet. That clock is not ours to control.
Migration of years of messy historical data. That is its own piece of work and it deserves its own estimate.
Anything needing formal certification or validation.
A feature list assembled by asking twenty people what they would like.

body.text: The conditions
Four weeks is not a property of the studio. It is a property of the project, and it holds when three things are true.

First, one person can make decisions. Not a committee, not a steering group, one person who can look at a screen and say yes or change it. The single biggest cause of overrun in small projects is not technical, it is waiting for an answer.

Second, the scope was cut before it started. Everything we have shipped on time had a scoping call where things were removed. That conversation is uncomfortable for about ten minutes and it saves a month.

Third, the client sees it weekly. A link every Friday means a wrong assumption is corrected in week two instead of discovered in week four. It is not a progress report, it is a correction mechanism, and it is why fixed price is survivable at all.
What happens when it slips

Sometimes it does. The usual reasons are an integration we were told was available and was not, a decision maker who went quiet, or something genuinely harder than it looked. The first two are about access and availability, which is why we write down what we need from the client at the start. The third one is ours, and on a fixed price it costs us rather than you. That is the entire point of quoting fixed price: the risk sits with the party who can estimate.
A four week project is not fast because people work faster. It is fast because less was attempted and nothing waited.

title: Custom software or off the shelf? A simple way to decide
excerpt: Off the shelf tools are cheaper on day one. Custom software is cheaper on day five hundred. Here is a plain test for which one your business actually needs.

body.text: Every growing business hits the same moment. The tool you signed up for in year one starts bending the way you work instead of the other way round. People keep side spreadsheets. Someone becomes the unofficial expert in workarounds. The question arrives: do we find a better product, or do we build our own?
There is no universal answer, but there is a reliable way to decide. It comes down to one question: is this process a commodity, or is it how you win?
Buy when the process is the same everywhere

Payroll, email, accounting, video calls. These work more or less the same in every company, and the products built for them are excellent because millions of customers shaped them. Building your own version would cost more and deliver less. Buy these, configure them well, and move on.
Build when the process is what makes you different

How you quote a job, allocate a crew, approve a purchase or track a site inspection is often specific to your business. That is exactly where off the shelf tools struggle, because they are built for the average company, and your advantage lives in the parts that are not average.

items: Your team keeps a spreadsheet next to the official tool
The same information is typed into two or three systems
Approvals happen in chat because the tool cannot model them
You pay for a large platform and use ten percent of it
Reports are built by hand before every meeting

body.text: If three or more of these sound familiar, the tool is costing you more in workarounds than it saves in licence fees.
The middle path most people miss

It is rarely all or nothing. The best setups keep the commodity tools and add a small custom layer on top: one app for the process that matters, connected to the systems you already pay for. You keep your accounting package and your CRM. You stop forcing them to do a job they were never designed for.
Buy for the parts of the business that look like everyone else. Build for the parts that make you you.
What it should cost you to find out

Not much. A good studio should be able to tell you in one short call whether a custom build makes sense, and if it does not, say so. If the answer is yes, the first release should be scoped tightly enough to ship in weeks, so you learn quickly whether it was the right call.

title: What your first release should include, and what it should not
excerpt: The first version of an app has one job: prove that people will use it. Everything that does not serve that job can wait for version two.

body.text: The most common way a software project goes wrong is not bad code. It is a first release that tries to do everything. It takes four months instead of four weeks, and by the time it launches, the problem has moved.
A first release has one job: put a working tool in real hands and prove people will use it. Here is how we decide what makes the cut.
Must have on day one

items: The one workflow that causes the most pain today, working end to end
Sign in, with the right people seeing the right things
The data you already have, brought across so nobody starts from zero
A way to see what is happening, even if it is one simple screen
Works on a phone, because that is where half your team will open it

body.text: Can wait for version two

items: Every edge case the team can imagine
Custom themes, animations and settings pages
Integrations with systems that only one person uses
Advanced reports nobody has asked for yet
Features that exist because a competitor has them

body.text: None of these are bad ideas. They are simply better decided after launch, when real use tells you which ones matter.
Ship the smallest thing that removes the biggest headache. Then listen.
A quick test

For every feature on the list, ask: if this was missing on launch day, would people stop using the app? If the honest answer is no, it goes on the version two list. That list is not a graveyard. It is the plan for the next few weeks, informed by people actually using the thing.

title: How we price fixed price projects, and why it protects you
excerpt: Hourly billing rewards the builder for taking longer. Fixed price puts the risk where it belongs. Here is exactly how we arrive at a number.

body.text: When a project is billed by the hour, every surprise is your problem. The estimate was forty hours, it took ninety, and the invoice follows the hours. You carry the risk of a job you cannot see inside.
We work the other way. Every project has a price agreed in writing before work begins. Here is how we get there, and what it means for you.
Step one: a short scoping call
We ask about the process, who uses it, what systems it touches and what good looks like on day one. Most of the time, twenty to thirty minutes is enough.
Step two: a written scope
Within a few days you receive a short document: what gets built, what it does on launch, what is deliberately left for later, the timeline in weeks, and the price. No jargon and no padding.
Step three: the price holds

If something takes us longer than planned, that is our problem, not yours. The only thing that changes the price is a change to the scope, and that is always your decision, agreed in writing before any extra work starts.

items: You know the full cost before you commit
You can compare it honestly against other options
There are no surprise invoices mid project
Changes are visible, deliberate and priced upfront

body.text: A fixed price is a promise. It forces both sides to agree on what done looks like before the work starts.
Why this works for us too
It keeps us honest about scope. If we cannot describe the first release clearly enough to price it, it is not ready to build yet, and it is far better to find that out on a call than in week six.

title: A field guide to scoping a two week app sprint
excerpt: The fastest way to blow a two week timeline is to scope three workflows and call it one. Here is exactly how we narrow a request down to something that actually ships on time.

body.text: Almost every project that comes to us starts the same way: we need an app for tracking X. By the end of a twenty minute call, X has usually split into three or four different things wearing one name.
The tell that a scope is too big

If a workflow needs more than one type of user with meaningfully different permissions, more than one approval stage, and more than one system it has to talk to, it is not one sprint. It is two, and trying to force it into one is how a two week estimate becomes an eight week apology.
What we actually ask on the call

items: Who logs the first entry, and what do they see on day one?
Who approves it, and what happens if they reject it?
Where does the data need to end up: a dashboard, an export, or another system entirely?
What is the one thing that, if it did not work on day one, would make this a failure?

body.text: That last question does more work than the other three combined. It forces a client to name the actual point of the app, instead of the wish list around it.
What gets cut, and why that is good news

Almost every scoping call ends with something removed, not added: the export nobody actually opens monthly, the second approval tier that exists on paper but never triggers in practice, the dashboard view that was requested before anyone had data to put in it. Cutting these is not a downgrade. It is the difference between a tool your team opens every day and a feature nobody remembers to use.

A sprint that ships in two weeks is not a smaller version of what you asked for. It is the sharpest version of what you actually need, with everything that was not load bearing removed before the first line of code.

title: Approvals over WhatsApp: the compliance risk nobody has written down
excerpt: If your approval trail lives in a chat thread, you do not have an approval process. You have a conversation that happened to end well, so far.

body.text: Ask most operations teams how a request gets approved and the honest answer, after enough follow up questions, is a WhatsApp thread or an email chain. Someone asks, someone with authority replies with a thumbs up or a one line yes, and everyone moves on.
Why this works right up until it does not

It works because the people involved trust each other and the decisions are usually correct. It stops working the moment anyone needs to answer a very specific question: who approved this, exactly when, under what version of the request, and what did they actually see before they said yes.
Where this becomes expensive

items: A disputed invoice, where the only evidence of sign off is a message that has since been deleted or a phone that has since been replaced.
A safety incident, where an auditor wants a documented approval chain and finds a text message instead.
A vendor payment approved by someone who was, on paper, not authorized to approve it, and nobody can say who actually gave the go ahead.

body.text: None of this means the team is careless. It means the approval process was never built as a process. It grew, informally, out of whatever tool was fastest to open.
What an approvals app actually buys you

Not more bureaucracy. The opposite: a request moves through the same number of steps it does today, but each step is logged, timestamped and tied to a specific person's login instead of a phone number. When an auditor or a dispute asks the question, the answer already exists, instead of needing to be reconstructed from memory and screenshots.

title: Why your Oracle Fusion backlog is six months long
excerpt: Your ERP partner is not incompetent. They are booked. Here is what is actually happening behind that ticket, and the one move that gets a workflow live without waiting for the queue to clear.

body.text: Every Ops or IT manager we talk to describes the same thing in almost the same words. A request goes into the Oracle Fusion partner's queue: one new screen, one workflow, one report that does not exist yet. Six months later, it still has not shipped.
The queue is not a bug

Your Fusion partner is not sitting on your ticket out of neglect. Their business runs on module implementations and large change orders, the kind of work priced in the hundreds of thousands. A one-screen violation tracker for your HSSE team is real work, but it is small work, and small work gets scheduled around the big contracts, not ahead of them. That is not a service failure. It is how the incentives are built.
What gets fast-tracked, and what does not

items: Anything tied to a paid module go-live moves first.
Anything billed under a retainer moves next, in the order it was opened.
A standalone request for one screen or one workflow, from a team that is not the one paying the big invoice, moves last.

body.text: If your request falls into that third bucket, it is not that nobody wants to help you. It is that you are, structurally, at the back of every queue that partner runs.
The workaround that actually works

The fix is not to escalate harder or find a more responsive partner. It is to stop asking your ERP partner to build small, standalone tools at all, and instead have someone build the workflow as a lightweight app that reads and writes to Oracle Fusion through its API. Your Fusion instance stays exactly as it is. The workflow your team actually needs shows up in two to four weeks instead of two to four quarters.
This is the entire premise behind an Oracle Fusion Bridge sprint: one workflow, scoped tightly, connected to the system you already run, built by someone whose only job that month is your ticket.
The problem was never Oracle Fusion. It was asking a platform built for enterprise-wide rollouts to also handle a single team's Tuesday morning workflow.
If you are staring down a backlog right now, the question worth asking is not when the ticket will move. It is whether it needs to be a ticket at all.

title: Fleet inspections on paper: what it is actually costing you
excerpt: A paper checklist feels free. It is not. It is a two day reconciliation job wearing a clipboard.

body.text: A paper vehicle inspection checklist is the cheapest possible way to start tracking fleet condition, and for a small fleet it is a reasonable way to run things. Past a certain size, the same paper checklist becomes the most expensive part of the process, just in a way that never appears on an invoice.
The hidden reconciliation tax

Someone, usually a fleet coordinator, spends one to two days a week turning stacks of paper checklists into a spreadsheet a regional manager can actually read. That is not fleet management. That is data entry wearing a fleet manager's job title.
What gets lost in the gap

items: A vehicle that failed an inspection on Tuesday keeps running until Friday, because the paper has not been transcribed yet.
Two supervisors report the same defect on two different vehicles, and nobody notices the pattern until a third one fails the same way.
The regional report presented in Monday's meeting is, structurally, four to six days out of date by the time anyone reads it.

body.text: A digital inspection app closes that gap by design, not by discipline. The inspection is the record. There is no second step where someone re-types it into the system that actually matters.

For a fleet running Oracle Fusion or another ERP for asset tracking, the app does not replace that system. It feeds it, in real time, from the one place the data actually gets created: the vehicle, at the moment someone is standing in front of it.

title: The real cost of tracking HSSE observations in a spreadsheet
excerpt: A spreadsheet does not fail loudly. It fails quietly, one overwritten row and one missed follow-up at a time, until an audit finds the gap for you.

body.text: Ask an HSSE manager how observations get logged and most describe the same system: a shared Excel file, one column per site, one row per incident, updated by whoever got to the laptop first that week.
Where it actually breaks

items: Two people editing the same file at once, and one set of entries quietly overwriting the other.
A site supervisor logging an observation on a phone, in a text message, meaning to add it to the sheet later.
No enforced closure. A hazard gets logged as open and nobody owns turning it into closed.
No trend visibility. Nobody can say, in a five minute glance, whether near misses are rising on a specific site.

body.text: Why this stays hidden until it does not

None of this shows up as a problem in a normal month. It shows up the day an auditor asks for a closure trail on a specific incident from four months ago, and the only record is a cell that somebody overwrote in March.
What replaces it

An HSSE observation tracker does three things a spreadsheet cannot: it enforces who can log, edit and close an observation, it timestamps every change instead of quietly overwriting the last one, and it gives a site or regional manager a live view instead of a monthly export. Built as a real app, wired into the same Oracle Fusion or ERP instance your compliance team already reports out of, it becomes the system of record instead of a side file nobody trusts.
None of this requires ripping out anything you already run. It requires one workflow, built once, used every day.
